considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), 0), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(capx, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(xrd, SUB(revt, revt)), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(TREND(LOG(sale), 3)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Persistently profitable firms that maintain high combined physical and R&D investment while sales trend downward earn lower subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: The signal captures an aggregate organic-investment push undertaken despite weakening demand, rather than assuming that either capex or R&D growth is independently excessive. SUMRANK avoids an excessively narrow three-way tail while the sales trend supplies an economically separate demand-validation test.

considered.name: Capital Obsolescence Churn
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)), 0), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ppegt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(ppent, 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Persistently profitable firms whose gross PPE expands while net PPE contracts earn lower subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Opposite movements in gross and net productive assets indicate that additions are being overwhelmed by depreciation, retirements, or obsolescence, revealing costly capital churn rather than productive capacity growth. This replaces previously unsuccessful margin and liquidity add-ons with a direct accounting measure of whether investment is forming durable net capacity.

considered.name: Dual-Channel Intangible Expansion
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), 0), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(intan, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(xrd, SUB(revt, revt)), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Persistently profitable firms that simultaneously increase capitalized intangible assets and expensed R&D earn lower subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Investors may extrapolate both current profitability and a broad innovation narrative when intangible investment rises through two accounting channels at once. Requiring concurrent capitalized and expensed investment distinguishes innovation exuberance from the previously tested crowding-out mechanisms and may capture overvaluation not represented by FF5 investment factors.

considered.name: Profit-Eroding Capacity Substitution
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)), 0), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(ppegt, 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(revt, cogs), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Persistently gross-profitable firms that replace productive capacity with inventory while gross profit declines earn lower subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Declining gross profit confirms that the shift from fixed capacity toward inventory is not a benign capital reallocation but an operating deterioration. This combines the strong abnormal-return evidence for capacity substitution with a realized-payoff failure rather than another cash-depletion condition.

considered.name: Innovation-Starved Capacity Substitution
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)), 0), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(ppegt, 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(xrd, SUB(revt, revt)), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Persistently gross-profitable firms that accumulate inventory, shrink productive capacity, and reduce R&D earn lower subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: The signal identifies broad deterioration in investment composition: resources move into working capital while both productive capacity and organic innovation retreat. Requiring R&D contraction distinguishes strategic short-termism from the distress-only interpretation of inventory-for-capacity substitution.

considered.name: Profit-Eroding Replacement Trap
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)), 0), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, at), 5)), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(ppent, 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(TREND(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Historically profitable firms with capex near its own historical high, shrinking net PPE, and deteriorating operating profitability earn lower subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: High capex that fails to form net capacity indicates replacement pressure or failed projects, while declining operating profitability confirms that the spending is not preserving productive economics. The payoff-failure condition is designed to strengthen the weak cross-sectional evidence of the replacement trap without relying on previously unsuccessful margin or liquidity add-ons.

considered.name: Dual Capital Starvation
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), 0), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(capx, dp), ppent)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(xrd, SUB(revt, revt)), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Persistently cash-profitable firms that underinvest in physical maintenance while reducing R&D earn lower subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Simultaneous maintenance deferral and innovation cuts indicate broad capital starvation rather than conservative growth or efficient cash harvesting. The two-leg construction tests whether the strong undermaintenance effect is especially persistent when firms also sacrifice long-horizon intangible investment.

considered.name: Acquisition Integration Cost Overrun
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), 0), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(aqc, LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(xsga, sale), 1), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Persistently profitable firms that spend heavily on acquisitions while SG&A intensity rises earn lower subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Rising SG&A intensity following acquisitive investment indicates integration costs, organizational duplication, or failure to realize expected overhead synergies. This tests a realized acquisition-cost mechanism rather than blending previously evaluated capex, acquisition, and R&D-crowding signals.

considered.name: Short-Funded Long-Horizon Innovation
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), 0), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(xrd, SUB(revt, revt)), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), LAG(at, 1)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Persistently profitable firms that increase R&D while financing with additional short-term debt earn lower subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: R&D is a long-duration, uncertain investment, so funding its expansion with short-maturity borrowing creates a refinancing mismatch even when current profitability is strong. The signal introduces an innovation-financing horizon mechanism rather than averaging previously tested visible-investment channels.

critic_notes.rationale: The MIN conjunction is a legitimate non-linear composite, but the two ingredients are near-textbook cash-based profitability (Novy-Marx) and abnormal capital investment (Titman-Wei-Xie), so the signal risks being little more than a double-sort of two known anomalies with modest incremental content.

The expression matches the stated conditional hypothesis and the profitability×investment interaction is economically motivated (q-theory implies exactly this), but multiplying a non-negative IND_RANK by a 0/1 indicator dumps all below-median-profitability firms into the bottom of the signal distribution, contaminating the short leg with a heterogeneous mass point rather than cleanly isolating low-growth profitable firms.

A genuinely cross-theme construct — realized profit growth benchmarked against the firm's own prior committed capacity growth — that is internally consistent and not a repackaging of a standard investment or profitability anomaly, though the unwinsorized growth ratios (especially oibdp with small or negative bases) and the mass point at zero for non-expanders need careful handling.

Scaling acquisition spend by internally generated cash rather than assets is a defensible refinement of the acquirer-underperformance and investment literature, but the oancf>0 filter binds on the large majority of firms so the "conditional" framing is largely cosmetic, and aqc is zero or missing for most firm-years, which will concentrate the signal in a thin, unstable subsample.

Positive gross profit is true for nearly all firms, so the "conditional" wrapper is essentially vacuous and the signal reduces to an inventory-change measure — a direct rediscovery of the well-documented inventory growth anomaly (Thomas-Zhang; Belo-Lin) with only a scaling variation.

With ib>0 for the majority of firm-years the conditioning adds little, leaving (capx − oancf)/at, which is simply negated free cash flow scaled by assets and is already spanned by the external-financing, accruals, and investment anomalies; the hypothesized "narrative vulnerability" story is not distinguishable from those known effects by this expression.

This is essentially the archive's "Equity-Funded Profitable Expansion" with the equity-issuance leg deleted, leaving a plain capex-growth (Titman-Wei-Xie capital investment) anomaly conditioned on profitability — a known effect and a cosmetic simplification rather than a substantively new mechanism.

The construction is a one-variable swap (invt→emp) on the archive's "Profitable Inventory Divergence" template and the primary driver, employment growth, is a well-published hiring-rate anomaly, so incremental content is limited and annual `emp` coverage will further thin an already sparse conditional sample.

The two legs individually recycle known effects (acquisitiveness/goodwill growth and earnings-versus-cash-flow divergence, i.e., accruals), but the conjunction conditional on persistent profitability is a coherent and internally consistent test that differs materially from the failed "Acquisition Cash Drain," though `gdwl` reporting gaps make coverage a real risk.

This is a rescaling (percentage growth → lagged-asset-scaled deltas) of the archive's weak "Installed Capacity Payoff Gap" with no new economic content, and the claim that zeroed non-expanders are "neutral" is unverified since a z-score difference need not have a median of zero within the traded cross-section.

A nested MIN of cash profitability, debt reduction, and investment restraint is a rediscovery of the standard quality/conservative-financing composite (profitability, net debt issuance, asset growth) and substantially overlaps the archive's "Renewal Surplus Conjunction," whose FMB slope already failed to translate into portfolio alpha.

Investment-policy instability conditioned on strong cash profitability is a genuinely distinct construct from the level/growth signals in the archive and the expression matches the stated sign, though a three-observation VOL is a noisy variance estimate that may proxy for size or capex level rather than discipline.

This is a near-clone of the archived "Profitable Inventory Divergence" (identical conditioning gate, identical inventory-growth leg, only the second leg swapped from gross-profit-change-to-assets to gross-margin change), i.e., precisely the cosmetic variant the objective warns against, and both legs also lean on the already-published inventory-growth and margin-deterioration anomalies.

The absolute-deviation-from-maintenance-capex leg is a genuinely non-monotonic reformulation of the investment channel (not just "less capex is better"), it is internally consistent with the positive expected sign, and it plausibly diagnoses the asset-stripping contamination that flipped the earlier Renewal Surplus portfolio evidence — though the ABS(capx−dp)/ppent term will be very noisy for asset-light firms even after winsorization.

The two legs are mechanically entangled — rising capex directly inflates the ppent denominator of sale/ppent, so "declining sales per unit of PPE" is partly implied by the first leg, meaning the conjunction risks collapsing into a double-counted investment-growth (asset-growth anomaly) signal rather than the claimed independent utilization channel.

Internally consistent and economically coherent, and debt-maturity funding is a substantively different channel from the archived equity-funded version, but it reuses that signal's exact template and both legs are close cousins of the well-documented asset-growth and net-debt-issuance anomalies, so incremental novelty is modest.

Expression matches the hypothesis and sign (high MIN = capex near own 5-year high while profitability sits well below its own peak), and using firm-specific historical position/peak distance rather than short-window ACCEL/TREND is a real measurement change from the archived Post-Peak Capex Commitment, not a relabeling.

The aging proxy is largely an accounting consequence of the first leg — sustained capex below depreciation mechanically raises accumulated depreciation and hence ppegt/ppent — so the "conjunction" is substantially redundant and may simply re-sort the same underinvestment variable that already failed to deliver alpha, even though the diagnostic motivation is sensible.

This is a cosmetic re-timing of the archived "Undermaintenance Profit Erosion" (same profitability gate, same capex-minus-depreciation leg, with the 3-year profitability trend swapped for a 1-year delta and both legs lagged), so it is effectively a rediscovery of an already-tested signal rather than a new mechanism.

The volatility leg is a near-substitute for the archived and unsuccessful "Profitable Capex Instability," and the combination of profitability conditioning with earnings volatility and capital intensity largely re-packages the well-documented earnings-volatility/asset-tangibility anomalies rather than testing a genuinely new interaction.

This is the archived "Profitable Inventory Divergence" — the pair's strongest result — with the gate and inventory leg lagged one year; the shift adds a plausible timing story but is too close to the original to count as a distinct test, and inventory growth is itself a canonical published anomaly.

The cash-depletion leg is a genuinely new ingredient relative to the archived post-peak capex signals and the sign logic is internally consistent, but the four-way conjunction (gate plus triple MIN) risks thin, unstable extreme portfolios and a large indicator-induced mass at zero, so coverage and turnover diagnostics must be checked carefully.

Mechanically coherent and sign-consistent, but it is the third variant of the same profitable-borrower/interest-expense theme that already yielded essentially zero FF5 alpha twice, and the second leg is contaminated by the profit-deterioration channel (a firm with falling oibdp and flat xint scores high), so it partly re-tests earnings decline rather than debt service.

Replacing the failed amortization-gap leg with a change in SG&A intensity is a substantively different cost channel rather than a cosmetic tweak, though ΔSG&A-to-sales overlaps the long-known Abarbanell–Bushee fundamental-signal literature, so the novelty rests mainly on the conditional interaction with intangible accumulation.

The construct is internally consistent and correctly signed, but netting Δcapx against Δcash and swapping a 3-year profitability trend for a one-period delta is largely a re-parameterization of the archive's best signal (Liquidity-Depleting Post-Peak Expansion) rather than a new mechanism, and the subtraction also allows a large cash build to be offset by a large capex cut, blurring the intended "resource pressure" interpretation.

This is a single-operator mutation (NEG→ABS) of the archive's Undermaintenance Profit Erosion, and because ABS pools two economically opposite groups—overinvestors and undermaintainers—any negative slope will most likely be inherited from the already-documented undermaintenance tail in diluted form, while the positive-sign evidence from Maintenance-Balanced Cash Generator makes the pooled hypothesis hard to interpret either way.

A three-year sum of capex/at is essentially the well-known capital-investment/asset-growth anomaly in level form, and pairing it with a declining profitability trend reproduces the structure of the archive's Post-Peak Capex Commitment and Peak-Profit Capex Lag (both weak), so this offers little incremental information.

Substituting firm-specific distance from a log-sales peak for the previously tested profitability-peak distance introduces genuinely different information (demand recession rather than margin erosion), the expression matches the stated hypothesis and sign, and the denominator-free demand measure sensibly avoids the capex-inflated-asset confound.

The cash-conversion leg is mechanically contaminated because oiadp is after depreciation while oancf adds it back, so capex-heavy firms with rising D&A tend to have a *falling* oiadp−oancf gap—working against the very conjunction the MIN requires—and the archive's oibdp-based Goodwill Cash Conversion Break already tested the cleaner version with negligible alpha.

The hypothesis is economically sensible, but the triple MIN over falling cash, falling operating income, and falling capex will be dominated by the deteriorating-fundamentals legs—effectively a distress/profitability-decline signal already spanned by known anomalies—and the fact that the exact opposite capex direction "worked" in the archive winner suggests the capex leg carries little independent information at very thin coverage.

The construction is internally consistent and the sign flip is evidence-motivated, but with two archive entries (Undermaintenance Profit Erosion, Demand-Validated Lean Capacity) already showing that the NEG((capx−dp)/ppent) leg drives negative returns regardless of the second conditioner, swapping sales growth for a five-year sales rank is a third re-test of the same underinvestment effect rather than a substantively new mechanism.

Recasting the archive's best signal (Liquidity-Depleting Post-Peak Expansion) in firm-specific historical levels rather than noisy one-year changes is a defensible, economically motivated reformulation and effectively fuses the Peak-Profit Capex Lag and Working-Capital Squeeze legs, though a three-way MIN on ~8% coverage risks a thin, unstable extreme portfolio and the improvement may prove measurement-cosmetic.

The diagnosis is sound — Profitable Expansion Breadth had a strong FMB slope but no alpha, plausibly because it captured the CMA investment factor — and requiring firm-specific demand retreat is a genuine attempt to isolate overbuild, but note that adding a third MIN leg does not remove the investment-factor loading from the long side and will further compress coverage.

This is the only proposal introducing a genuinely new input (emp) and a distinct sticky-labor mechanism, and the sales-below-peak conditioner meaningfully differentiates it from the published hiring-rate anomaly, though TS_RANK(emp,5) is close to monotone in cumulative employment growth so the conditioning leg must carry real incremental information for the signal to be more than a repackaged hiring-rate sort.

This is a component swap on Short-Funded Capacity Expansion (invt for ppegt, gross profit for oibdp gate), a construct that already delivered essentially zero FF5 alpha (−0.000, t=−0.008), and both legs are separately covered by Profitable Inventory Divergence and Profitable Expansion Breadth, so it is a cosmetic variant of tested and portfolio-unsuccessful ideas.

The expected negative sign fights two well-established published effects simultaneously — the low-investment/low-asset-growth premium (already spanned by FF5's CMA) and the high-cash-holdings return premium — and the only supporting evidence is the statistically insignificant Liquidity-Restoring Investment Reset (t=−0.99), making this a level-based sign flip of an already-tested construct rather than a new mechanism.

This is a mechanical recombination of two legs already tested in the archive — the inventory TS_RANK leg from "Profitable Working-Capital Squeeze" and the sales-peak-distance leg from "Demand-Peak Investment Rigidity"/"Broad Expansion Into Demand Retreat" — under the identical gross-profitability gate, so it offers no new economic content beyond leg swapping.

This is exactly "Historical Liquidity Overcommitment" with the third (profitability-below-peak) leg deleted, a strict subset of an already-evaluated signal rather than a substantively different construction, and dropping the discriminating leg is more likely to dilute than sharpen the effect.

The construct is close to "Demand-Validated Lean Capacity" with the expected sign flipped to match that signal's realized (contrary) result, and the stated mechanism — that capacity contraction predicts *low* returns — directly contradicts the well-documented asset-growth/investment anomaly without a persuasive reason why near-peak sales should reverse it, so the sign looks fitted rather than theorized.

The diagnosis is legitimate — "Profitable Expansion Breadth" had a strong slope but negligible FF5 alpha, plausibly an investment-factor loading, and the cash-depletion leg is the same ingredient that made "Liquidity-Depleting Post-Peak Expansion" the archive's best performer — but it remains an incremental third-leg addition whose main risk is coverage thinning and overlap with that earlier winner.

TS_RANK of raw employment levels is mechanically near its maximum for any firm with secular headcount growth, so the first leg is largely a hiring-rate proxy and thus close to the published employment-growth anomaly, and the cash-rank leg was already tested in the archive's working-capital and liquidity-overcommitment signals.

Requiring opposite-signed movements in working versus fixed capital is a genuinely different construct from the archive's same-direction expansion conjunctions and is not a simple restatement of asset growth, though the researcher should verify the extreme portfolio is not dominated by distressed asset-sale cases and check whether the two legs' opposing known return signs leave any net predictive content.

This is a cosmetic aggregation variant of the already-tested "Liquidity-Funded Expansion Breadth" (identical three legs, MIN→SUMRANK on the two investment terms only), so it changes the tail-thinning mechanics without introducing any new economic content.

Adding cash depletion to the inventory-up/capacity-down conjunction is a substantive economic discriminator (distress-driven asset shedding vs. benign reallocation) rather than a relabeling, though the triple-MIN will thin the extreme portfolio and the incremental information over the parent signal may be modest.

TREND of invt/che is numerically pathological because cash can be arbitrarily close to zero (1% winsorization will not tame a 3-year trend of an exploding ratio), and the construct largely restates the already-tested "Profitable Working-Capital Squeeze" (high inventory, low cash) in continuous form.

The mechanism — high capex that produces neither net capacity nor retained liquidity — is coherent and the sign logic is internally consistent, but it repeats the same "bolt on NEG(DELTA(che))" move used elsewhere in this batch and builds on a parent whose cross-sectional slope was already weak (fmb −1.10).

Rescaling aqc by che rather than at is essentially a denominator swap on a parent signal that already failed (fmb −0.81), and che is a near-zero-prone scaler that will make the ratio's cross-sectional distribution unstable and winsorization-dependent rather than a cleaner measure of balance-sheet stretch.

The hypothesis (capital deepening that fails to deliver overhead relief signals unproductive investment) is economically clean and the expression matches the stated sign, but both legs have already been tested in adjacent combinations with weak results, so this is a plausible-but-low-prior recombination rather than a new mechanism.

This is the archive's strongest signal (Profitable Inventory Divergence) with the now-formulaic NEG(DELTA(che)) third leg bolted on — a template already applied four separate times in the archive (Liquidity-Depleting Post-Peak Expansion, Liquidity-Funded Expansion Breadth, Distressed Working-Capital Substitution, Liquidity-Draining Replacement Trap) — so it is a cosmetic extension rather than a new mechanism, and MIN-narrowing a leg that already delivers t=-4.9 is more likely to dilute than sharpen.

Identical construction pattern to the previous proposal — Tangible Expansion Crowds Out Innovation plus the reused cash-depletion leg — and no argument is offered for why liquidity strain is economically distinct from the capex-increase leg it is being conjoined with (rising capex mechanically drains cash), so the third leg risks being redundant rather than informative.

The reasoning correctly diagnoses the strong-slope/weak-alpha problem of Profitable Expansion Breadth as CMA overlap and substitutes a realized-payoff-failure leg rather than another liquidity leg, though the resulting expression is close to Profitable Inventory Divergence with a ppegt leg appended, so incremental information over the archive's best signal is uncertain.

The margin-trend leg has already been directly tested in Fixed-Capacity Margin Squeeze and was essentially dead (fmb -0.05, ls_talpha 0.28), and adding a third leg to Capex Without Capacity Formation was already tried (Liquidity-Draining Replacement Trap) with no gain, so this combines two known-unhelpful modifications and will most likely just shrink the sample.

Same reused cash-depletion-leg template applied to a weak base (Inventory-Backed Margin Inflation, fmb -1.78, ls_talpha -0.90), and the hypothesis is internally strained because the overproduction story implies margins rise from cost deferral while cash falls from inventory build — two symptoms of the same accounting event, not independent confirmation.

This is a genuinely distinct two-leg mechanism (purchased versus internally developed innovation) that is not a rediscovery of any archive signal and whose expected negative sign follows naturally from both legs, with the caveats that COALESCE-to-zero makes non-R&D reporters indistinguishable from true R&D cutters and that aqc's sparsity may limit coverage.

This is essentially a SUMRANK blend of two already-tested archive signals ("Working Capital Crowds Out Innovation" and "Tangible Expansion Crowds Out Innovation") with the identical R&D-decline leg and profitability gate, so it is a cosmetic averaging of known results rather than a new mechanism and will most likely just interpolate their existing t-stats.

The swap of a realized gross-profit-decline leg for the previously tested cash-depletion leg is a defensible payoff-validation refinement of the capacity-substitution family, though it overlaps heavily with both "Distressed Working-Capital Substitution" and the gen-0 "Profitable Inventory Divergence" and mildly double-counts gross profitability as both gate and leg.

The triple intersection of inventory build, capacity contraction, and R&D retrenchment is a genuinely untested combination whose legs are individually supported, but it is highly derivative of two neighboring archive entries and risks being driven mainly by the R&D leg rather than the substitution story.

Adding a profitability-trend deterioration leg is a substantive (not cosmetic) attempt to fix the weak cross-sectional evidence of "Capex Without Capacity Formation," though conditioning on persistently above-industry profitability while simultaneously requiring a falling profitability trend narrows the sample toward an internally tense subset and the capex-TS_RANK family has consistently produced weak fmb t-stats.

Pairing sub-depreciation physical investment with R&D contraction is the most genuinely new leg combination here and tests a coherent "broad capital starvation" mechanism, with the main caveat that archive evidence suggests the undermaintenance leg alone may carry most of the predictive power and coverage will be thin (~0.08) due to the ppent denominator.

Like the first proposal, this merely SUMRANK-averages the visible-investment legs of two already-evaluated signals ("Buy-Versus-Build Innovation Substitution" and "Tangible Expansion Crowds Out Innovation") while retaining the same R&D leg and gate, making it a rediscovery-by-blending with little incremental economic content.
